paras: The lynching of John Brooks took place at Jacksonville, Alabama, on October 5, 1882, when a large crowd took Brooks, a Black prisoner, from the sheriff after his preliminary hearing and hanged him on the outskirts of the town. Brooks had been accused of assaulting a little girl near Anniston, and a wire dispatch from Anniston carried the story to dailies across the country.

According to the Anniston dispatch, Brooks, called 'a burly negro', was accused of having 'brutally assaulted a little girl' on the outskirts of Anniston about ten days before; a Chattanooga Times special printed in Bismarck said two days. The Huntsville Gazette said only that he 'was charged with rape', and none of the reports named the girl. Brooks was captured on October 4 and lodged in the jail at Jacksonville.

On the afternoon of October 5 he was brought before a judge for a preliminary trial, at which, the dispatch said, he 'confessed his guilt', and the judge ordered him back to jail. A large crowd then took the prisoner 'out of the Sheriff's hands', carried him to the outskirts of the town and hanged him. The dispatch described the crowd as 'quiet and determined', and the Marietta Journal wrote that it 'hanged him until dead'. The coverage does not say where the crowd seized him, how many took part, or whether the sheriff resisted.

No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the crowd, or official comment appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named the sheriff, the judge or any lyncher. At the end of the year, chronologies of 1882 listed the case in one line as 'John Brooks, colored, hanged by a mob at Jacksonville, Ala.'.

The story reached the press as a single Anniston dispatch dated October 5, relayed through Chattanooga and printed the next day in the New-York Tribune, the New York Sun, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Memphis Daily Appeal and the Savannah Morning News. Northern papers used plain heads such as 'A Negro Lynched', while the Sacramento paper's 'Another Negro Taken from the Officials and Lynched' placed it in a series of such cases. Southern dailies framed it more sharply: the Memphis Daily Appeal headed it 'A Black Brute Hanged by a Mob' and the Savannah Morning News 'A Negro Fiend Lynched', and in the West the Bismarck Tribune called Brooks 'A Child Ravisher' and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer headed a shortened version 'Served Right'.

The only separately worded Alabama report, in the Huntsville Gazette of October 7, did not name Brooks and stated only that 'a mob took a prisoner from the custody of the Sheriff and hung him', adding that he 'was colored and was charged with rape'. Weekly news digests reduced the case to a line and often garbled it: the Brookings County Sentinel called Brooks 'a dusky libertine' taken from jail at Anniston, and a 'South and West' column in the Gloucester County Democrat placed the lynching at 'Jacksonville, Tenn.'. That column was still circulating in South Carolina's Abbeville Press and Banner on October 18.

The contemporary dispatches and the Huntsville Gazette put the lynching on October 5, a Thursday, while the Crawford Avalanche's year-end chronology listed it under October 4, the day of Brooks's capture. The dispatch placed the hearing and seizure in the afternoon, whereas the Huntsville Gazette wrote of 'the evening of the 5th'.

framing.detail: Southern dailies headed the dispatch 'A Black Brute Hanged by a Mob' and 'A Negro Fiend Lynched', and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer headed it 'Served Right'.
Northern dailies ran the dispatch under neutral heads such as 'A Negro Lynched' and 'Another Negro Taken from the Officials and Lynched'.
The Huntsville Gazette gave a one-sentence local item, without naming Brooks, stating only the charge and the mob's act.
Weekly digests compressed it to one line, one calling Brooks 'a dusky libertine', some misplacing it in Tennessee or Anniston.

versions.value: October 5 (Thursday), the day of the preliminary trial

conflicts.note: The Oct. 5 dispatches and the Alabama report are contemporary and agree on the 5th; the Crawford Avalanche chronology lists the 4th, and the True Northerner's '2' comes from its renumbered October list (Frank James's surrender of the 5th appears as '3'), so it is a numbering error.

versions.value: afternoon ('This afternoon', after the preliminary trial)

conflicts.note: The dispatch places the trial in the afternoon and the seizure after it; the Huntsville Gazette says evening.
Only the Bismarck version says two days.
The distant digests confuse the Anniston dateline and the state; the dispatch and the Alabama paper place jail and lynching at Jacksonville, Ala.
